Our ProjectOverview

Shadowfax is a courier service offering fast, reliable, and affordable delivery solutions. Recognizing the demand for remote services and providing convenient door-to-door delivery for individuals and businesses by saving time and resources in today's fast-paced economy. As the logistics sector rapidly grows, Shadowfax ensures efficient planning and execution from pickup to destination, supporting seamless business operations.

TheProblem Statement

Shadowfax App missed the mark by offering just one drop-off option, neglecting users' need for multiple delivery locations. This oversight led to a real drop in retention, as they switched to competitors. This highlights the crucial need for user-centric design, continuous iteration, and user feedback to improve functionality and satisfaction.

User drop-off

of users needing multiple drop-offs abandoned the app for a competitor rather than place separate single-drop orders.

Research: what users actually said

Interview quotes below are real, anonymized. Two are directly traceable to the personas that follow.

  • "I need a delivery service that's fast and reliable, I can't afford delays. My customers expect their packages on time, and it's crucial for keeping them happy and coming back."

    Business owner, multi-branch hardware retailer

  • "I want to know exactly where my packages are at all times. It's stressful not knowing if they're safe or when they'll arrive."

    Individual sender

  • "I need a logistics partner that can handle multiple deliveries across the country without breaking the bank or sacrificing service quality."

    Individual sender, frequent shipper

  • "When I ship delicate items like paintings, I worry about them getting damaged. I need a service that guarantees safe delivery, no matter how fragile the item."

    Independent artist & online seller

  • "Managing and shipping multiple orders shouldn't be a nightmare. I'm looking for a more efficient process that won't rack up unnecessary costs or create logistical headaches."

    Small business owner

Interview insights

  1. 1

    Time and cost efficiency are non-negotiable

    Users value courier speed and price highly, and delayed deliveries, lost items, and poor communication erode trust fast, both for personal senders and for the businesses that depend on them.

  2. 2

    Real-time tracking isn't a nice-to-have

    Not knowing where a package is, or when it'll arrive, was a recurring source of anxiety across nearly every interview.

  3. 3

    Multi-drop support is a scalability requirement

    Business users need a cost-effective way to support multiple deliveries per order, this is the gap the whole redesign centers on.

  4. 4

    Bulk order management is currently a manual headache

    Users managing several simultaneous orders have no efficient system for it today, costing them time and money.

How might we

Turning pain points into design challenges before moving to ideation.

1How might we optimize the delivery process to ensure timely and safe delivery of packages, enhancing customer trust and satisfaction for business users like Mr. Shah?
2How might we integrate end-to-end tracking to give users real-time visibility and peace of mind about their shipments' status?
3How might we design a cost-efficient logistics solution that supports multiple deliveries nationwide, for high-volume shippers like Mr. Shah?
4How might we develop specialized packaging and handling protocols for fragile items, so they reach customers like Rashi's in pristine condition?
5How might we simplify logistics management for small business owners like Rashi, making it easy to organize and ship multiple orders affordably?

Competitor Analysis

Explored why users lean towards our top three competitors over Shadowfax. Uncovered key insights by conducting user research and competitive analysis, identifying gaps in our service and design, then applied these findings to enhance our user experience and regain their preference.

Where the current app was losing people

One exhibit, cropped from the actual flow at full resolution so nothing is lost to a thumbnail, plus the full ten-screen flow below it as supporting evidence. Both come from the live product screens, not a mockup.

Exhibit AThe home screen has exactly one destination field

1
  1. 1
    Jakob's Law

    Pickup and "Search drop location" are the only two address fields anywhere on this screen. There is no third field, no "+" control, no affordance of any kind for a second stop. Every stop-based app a user already knows, Uber, Google Maps, treats multi-stop as a default, not an upsell, so this reads as broken, not minimal.

From sketch to two competing designs

Low-fidelity wireframes first, then two full high-fidelity variants built in parallel, so the usability test would have something real to compare instead of one design against a blank baseline.

The two variants share almost the entire flow. The one screen where they genuinely diverge is the very first one:

Miller's LawLaw of Common RegionFitts's LawRecognition rather than recall

The order flow is chunked into pickup, drop, item detail, and summary as separate screens rather than one long form, keeping what's on screen at once within working memory (Miller's Law). Within each screen, route info, item details, and payment each sit inside their own bordered card, so related fields read as one group without needing extra labels (Law of Common Region). Primary actions are full-width buttons anchored to the bottom of the screen, in easy thumb reach rather than requiring a stretch (Fitts's Law). And every address field opens onto a list of recent and saved addresses instead of asking the user to retype one (recognition rather than recall, Nielsen heuristic 6).

Validation: testing two designs, not defending one

Both variants went through moderated usability testing in Usability Hub, scored per screen for clarity and focus, plus click heatmaps.

ScreenVariant A (clarity/focus)Variant B (clarity/focus)Higher clarity
Home / pickup map 38 / 75 36 / 75 A
Pickup address form 60 / 75 56 / 75 A
Drop / landmark entry form 40 / 96 43 / 96 B
Order summary & route 56 / 63 56 / 63 Tie
Order summary & payment 48 / 96 40 / 96 A
Trip / drop details 65 / 76 65 / 76 Tie

Reading the two heatmap sets side by side: the split was close, not a landslide, A ahead on 3 of 6 screens, B on 1, tied on 2. Raw clarity scores alone don't settle it. Variant B is the version that shipped as the final design, and the reasons show up downstream of these six screens rather than in them: B's landing page doesn't force a Single/Multiple Drop decision before the user has even set a pickup point (see the comparison above), and B is the variant where the supporting flow was carried all the way through, a real address form with "select from contacts" and a Home/Office/Other address type, and a payment screen that itemizes every receiver by name and reference number instead of stopping at a drop count.

The fix, screen by screen

Six exhibits, same crop-and-callout treatment, matched directly against the gap in Exhibit A.

Exhibit B"+ Add New Stop" closes the Exhibit A gap directly

1
  1. 1
    Direct fix

    One tap on "Add New Stop" appends a second drop location to the same order, right below the first. This is the one control the entire before-flow never had.

Exhibit CA dedicated item-detail step, with fragile handling set apart

1
  1. 1
    Von Restorff EffectHMW 4

    "Please handle with care. Contains fragile item." sits in its own bordered text block, not folded into a generic notes field. This is the step that never existed in the before-flow, direct answer to Rashi’s interview quote about paintings getting damaged in transit.

Exhibit DThe order summary, now with a real number

1
  1. 1
    Direct fix

    "4 Drops" replaces the frozen "1 Drops" label from the before-flow, in the exact same layout slot (see the filmstrip above). The prototype’s delivery fee stays flat at ₹287 regardless of drop count, since real per-stop pricing logic was never modeled, but the fix that matters is structural: the order can now actually hold more than one destination.

Exhibit EThe flow ends on a clear confirmation, not a silent screen

1
  1. 1
    Peak-End Rule

    A plain "Delivered" banner plus a rating prompt closes every order. People judge a whole experience disproportionately by how it ends, so this is a deliberate last screen, not a default one.

Exhibit FThe address form grew up: contacts, address type, saved addresses

1
  1. 1
    Recognition rather than recall

    "Select from contacts" turns a name and phone number into a picker instead of two fields to retype by hand. Paired with it: a Home / Office / Other address type and an editable address name, so a repeat sender like Kamlesh never re-enters "Tower 9, Reliable Residency Layout" again. None of this existed in the before-flow’s address form, which had exactly four fields and nothing else.

Exhibit GCheckout itemizes every drop by name, not just a count

1
  1. 1
    Direct fix

    Four numbered receivers, each with their own address and reference number, replace the single, static "1 Drops" label from the before-flow. This is the same screen family, now actually carrying the data the order needs: four distinct people get four distinct hand-off references, not one order note split four ways.

One more thing doing real work across all six: the same orange, iconography, and tone carries through every screen, before and after. A more polished-feeling interface reads as more trustworthy before a user has tested a single feature (the Aesthetic-Usability Effect), which matters directly for an app whose core complaint was trust.

What the original process didn't cover

Naming this honestly matters more for a hiring case study than pretending the deck was complete. Three real gaps, worth fixing before calling this production-ready.

  • No accessibility pass.

    Nothing in the 26 slides checks color contrast (the orange-on-white CTA text is worth a WCAG contrast check), tap target sizing, or screen-reader labeling. For an app whose whole pitch is reliability, that's a real gap, not a nice-to-have.

  • No error or edge-case states.

    Every screen shown is a happy path. There's no design for a failed payment, no driver found, or a dropped connection mid-delivery, which is exactly where Nielsen's "help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors" heuristic should apply and currently doesn't.

  • No progress indicator across the multi-step order flow.

    Pickup → drop → item details → summary → payment is five screens deep with no visible step counter. The Goal-Gradient Effect (people push harder as they perceive themselves getting closer to a finish line) is sitting unused here, a simple step indicator is a likely completion-rate win the original design left on the table.

Outcome & reflection

This was a self-directed redesign, not a change shipped into Shadowfax's production app, so there's no live retention number to report. What is real: the interviews, two fully competing hi-fi variants instead of one design defended after the fact, and a usability test that picked the winning structure on clarity and focus scores rather than personal preference.

With more time, the next step is testing the final post-fix screens themselves, the multi-drop entry, scheduling, and fragile-item flagging, the same way the two variants were tested, to confirm they actually resolve what the original heatmaps flagged. Re-checking the 60% drop-off figure against a live cohort after the fix ships would be the real test of whether this closed the gap it was built for.

What this project demonstrates: a full research-to-validation loop on a real, measurable business problem. The final design's structure came from a scored comparison between two competing alternatives, decided by test data rather than by whichever concept got presented first.
